etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English bruisen, brusen, brosen, brisen, bresen, from a merger two words, both ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrews- (“to break”):

definitions.definition: (transitive) To strike (a person), originally with something flat or heavy, but now specifically in such a way as to discolour the skin without breaking it.

quote.citation: 1922, E[ric] R[ücker] Eddison, The Worm Ouroboros‎[1], London: Jonathan Cape, pages 25–26:
quote.text: It is as I have spoken: the testing first, next the bruising, and in the last bout the breaking and killing.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To damage the skin of (fruit or vegetables), in an analogous way.
(intransitive) Of fruit or vegetables, to gain bruises through being handled roughly.
(intransitive) To fight with the fists; to box.

quote.citation: 1854, Arthur Pendennis [pseudonym; William Makepeace Thackeray], The Newcomes: Memoirs of a Most Respectable Family, volume (please specify |volume=I or II), London: Bradbury and Evans, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Bruising was considered a fine, manly, old English custom.

definitions.definition: (transitive, figurative) To harm or injure somebody's feelings or self-esteem.
(transitive) To impair (gin) by shaking rather than stirring.
A purplish mark on the skin due to leakage of blood from capillaries under the surface that have been damaged by a blow.
A dark mark on fruit or vegetables caused by a blow to the surface.
